notes.front: What is metal corrosion?
notes.back: The deterioration of metal by chemical or electrochemical attack, inside the metal as well as on its surface.
notes.explanation: Like rot in wood, it can change the smooth surface, weaken the interior, or damage or loosen adjacent parts.
notes.example: Like a beam rotting from the inside, but in metal and driven by chemistry rather than fungus.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Factors Affecting Corrosion”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: Metal corrosion is the deterioration of the metal by chemical or electrochemical attack. This type of damage can take place internally, as well as on the surface. As in the rotting of wood, this deterioration may change the smooth surface, weaken the interior, or damage or loosen adjacent parts.

notes.front: What is electrochemical attack?
notes.back: Corrosion that needs a medium, usually water, able to conduct a tiny electric current between the metal and the corrosive agent.
notes.explanation: Corrosion begins, as the metal decays by oxidation, once a liquid or gaseous path that electrons flow through links the metal and the agent.
notes.example: Like a tiny battery, but the two terminals are two areas of an aircraft skin joined by a film of salt water.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: The reaction in this corrosive attack requires a medium, usually water, that is capable of conducting a tiny current of electricity. When a metal comes in contact with a corrosive agent and is also connected by a liquid or gaseous path that electrons flow through, corrosion begins as the metal decays by oxidation.

notes.front: What is direct chemical attack?
notes.back: Pure chemical corrosion caused by direct exposure of a bare surface to caustic liquid or gaseous agents.
notes.explanation: Unlike electrochemical attack, its anodic and cathodic changes happen at the same point and at the same time.
notes.example: Like acid eating into a bare metal surface it is poured on, with no current flowing between separate areas.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Direct Chemical Attack”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Direct chemical attack, or pure chemical corrosion, is an attack resulting from direct exposure of a bare surface to caustic liquid or gaseous agents. Unlike electrochemical attack where anodic and cathodic changes take place a measurable distance apart, the changes in direct chemical attack occur simultaneously at the same point.

notes.front: What is surface corrosion?
notes.back: The most common form of corrosion: a general roughening, etching or pitting of a metal surface, often with a powdery deposit.
notes.explanation: It is also called uniform etch or uniform attack corrosion, because it spreads over the surface as a whole.
notes.example: Like the dull, frosted patch that spreads over a neglected polished panel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Corrosion”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: General surface corrosion (also referred to as uniform etch or uniform attack corrosion) is the most common form of corrosion. Surface corrosion appears as a general roughening, etching, or pitting of the surface of a metal, frequently accompanied by a powdery deposit of corrosion products.

notes.front: What is filiform corrosion?
notes.back: An oxygen concentration cell under an organic coating, recognised by wormlike traces of corrosion products beneath the paint.
notes.explanation: The handbook treats it as a special form of oxygen concentration cell, found only on metal carrying an organic coating system.
notes.example: Like thin worm tracks raised under the paint of an aircraft parked by the sea.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Filiform Corrosion”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: Filiform corrosion is a special form of oxygen concentration cell that occurs on metal surfaces having an organic coating system. It is recognized by its characteristic wormlike trace of corrosion products beneath the paint film.

notes.front: What is pitting corrosion?
notes.back: One of the most destructive forms: tiny pits, first seen under a white or grey powdery deposit, most common on aluminium and magnesium alloys.
notes.explanation: It can occur in any metal, not only the alloys that form oxide films.
notes.example: Like a scatter of pinpricks in a sheet, each small at the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pitting Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: It can occur in any metal but is most common on metals that form protective oxide films, such as aluminum and magnesium alloys. It is first noticeable as a white or gray powdery deposit, similar to dust, which blotches the surface. When the deposit is cleaned away, tiny holes or pits can be seen in the surface.

notes.front: What is dissimilar metal corrosion?
notes.back: Galvanic action at contact points between dissimilar metal parts, in the presence of a conductor, where insulation has broken down or been omitted.
notes.explanation: It can cause extensive pitting damage whether or not surface corrosion is also taking place.
notes.example: Like a steel bolt through an aluminium bracket after the insulating layer between them has worn through.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Dissimilar Metal Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Extensive pitting damage may result from contact between dissimilar metal parts in the presence of a conductor. While surface corrosion may or may not be taking place, a galvanic action, not unlike electroplating, occurs at the points or areas of contact where the insulation between the surfaces has broken down or been omitted.

notes.front: What is concentration cell corrosion?
notes.back: Crevice corrosion: in a metal-to-metal joint, at the edge of a joint even of identical metals, or under foreign material on the surface.
notes.explanation: Unlike dissimilar metal corrosion, it does not need two different metals: the joined metals may be identical.
notes.example: Like corrosion hiding along the seam where two identical sheets overlap.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Concentration Cell Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Concentration cell corrosion, (also known as crevice corrosion) is corrosion of metals in a metal-to-metal joint, corrosion at the edge of a joint even though the joined metals are identical, or corrosion of a spot on the metal surface covered by a foreign material.

notes.front: What is intergranular corrosion?
notes.back: An attack along the grain boundaries of an alloy, commonly caused by a lack of uniformity in the alloy structure.
notes.explanation: Aluminium alloys and some stainless steels are particularly susceptible to it.
notes.example: Like mortar crumbling between bricks while the bricks themselves stay whole.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Intergranular Corrosion”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: This type of corrosion is an attack along the grain boundaries of an alloy and commonly results from a lack of uniformity in the alloy structure. Aluminum alloys and some stainless steels are particularly susceptible to this form of electrochemical attack.

notes.front: What is exfoliation corrosion?
notes.back: An advanced form of intergranular corrosion that lifts surface grains by the force of corrosion products expanding at the grain boundaries.
notes.explanation: It is the visible evidence of intergranular corrosion going on just below the surface.
notes.example: Like the pages of a soaked book swelling and peeling apart.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exfoliation Corrosion”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: Exfoliation corrosion is an advanced form of intergranular corrosion and shows itself by lifting up the surface grains of a metal by the force of expanding corrosion products occurring at the grain boundaries just below the surface. [Figure 8-15] It is visible evidence of intergranular corrosion

notes.front: What is stress-corrosion cracking?
notes.back: Cracking caused by a constant or cyclic stress acting together with a damaging chemical environment.
notes.explanation: The stress may come from internal or external loading.
notes.example: Like a rope under steady load that fails sooner once it is soaked in acid.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Stress-Corrosion/Cracking”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: This form of corrosion involves a constant or cyclic stress acting in conjunction with a damaging chemical environment. The stress may be caused by internal or external loading.

notes.front: What is fretting corrosion?
notes.back: Attack when two mating surfaces, normally at rest, have slight relative motion, pitting them and producing much fine debris.
notes.explanation: The restricted movement stops the debris escaping, so the abrasion stays extremely localised.
notes.example: Like a loose-fitting joint that grinds its own dust as it shivers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fretting Corrosion”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: occurs when two mating surfaces, normally at rest with respect to one another, are subject to slight relative motion. It is characterized by pitting of the surfaces and the generation of considerable quantities of finely divided debris. Since the restricted movements of the two surfaces prevent the debris from escaping very easily, an extremely localized abrasion occurs.

notes.front: What is fatigue corrosion?
notes.back: Failure under cyclic stress in a corrosive environment, where the stress level needed for failure may be reduced many times.
notes.explanation: Without a corrosive environment, the metal fails from fatigue only after its endurance limit is exceeded.
notes.example: Like a wire bent back and forth that snaps sooner when wet with salt water.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fatigue Corrosion”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: Once the limit has been exceeded, the metal eventually cracks and fails from metal fatigue. However, when the part or structure undergoing cyclic stress is also exposed to a corrosive environment, the stress level for failure may be reduced many times.

notes.front: What is galvanic corrosion?
notes.back: Corrosion when two dissimilar metals make electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte.
notes.explanation: Its rate depends on how far apart the two metals are in activity: the greater the difference, the faster the attack.
notes.example: Like a copper pipe joined straight to a steel one in a damp cellar.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Galvanic Corrosion”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Galvanic corrosion occurs when two dissimilar metals make electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte. [Figure 8-18] The rate which corrosion occurs depends on the difference in the activities. The greater the difference in activity, the faster corrosion occurs.

notes.front: What is the galvanic series of metals and alloys?
notes.back: A ranking of metals and alloys by electrical potential, or “nobility”; the less noble a metal, the more easily it corrodes.
notes.explanation: Every metal and alloy has a specific electrical potential in a given chemical environment, and the series orders them by it.
notes.example: Like a pecking order: in any pair of touching metals, the less noble one is the one that gets eaten.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: All metals and alloys are electrically active and have a specific electrical potential in a given chemical environment. This potential is commonly referred to as the metal’s “nobility.” [Figure 8-6] The less noble a metal is, the more easily it can be corroded.

notes.front: What are exhaust trail areas, as corrosion-prone areas?
notes.back: Areas downstream of exhaust pipes or nozzles, where corrosive exhaust deposits collect in gaps, seams, hinges and fairings.
notes.explanation: Both jet and reciprocating engine exhaust deposits are very corrosive.
notes.example: Like the soot streak behind a car exhaust, but settling into the skin seams behind an engine nacelle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exhaust Trail Areas”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: Both jet and reciprocating engine exhaust deposits are very corrosive and give particular trouble where gaps, seams, hinges, and fairings are located downstream from the exhaust pipes or nozzles.

notes.front: Why are battery compartments and vents treated as corrosion-prone areas?
notes.back: Fumes from overheated electrolyte are hard to contain and spread to nearby cavities, rapidly attacking unprotected metal.
notes.explanation: Better paint finishes, sealing and venting have not removed the problem.
notes.example: Like the white crust that grows round a car battery terminal, but spreading into the structure around it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Battery Compartments and Battery Vent Openings”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: Despite improvements in protective paint finishes and in methods of sealing and venting, battery compartments continue to be corrosion prone areas. Fumes from overheated electrolyte are difficult to contain and spread to adjacent cavities, causing a rapid corrosive attack on all unprotected metal surfaces.

notes.front: What is blending (or fairing) after corrosion removal?
notes.back: Smoothing every depression left by corrosion rework into the surrounding surface.
notes.explanation: It begins by removing rough edges and all corrosion from the damaged area.
notes.example: Like sanding a gouge in a tabletop into a shallow, smooth dish instead of leaving a sharp-edged hole.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fairing or Blending Reworked Areas”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: All depressions resulting from corrosion rework must be faired or blended with the surrounding surface. Fairing can be accomplished as follows: 1. Remove rough edges and all corrosion from the damaged area.

notes.front: What is anodising (spelt “anodizing” in the handbook)?
notes.back: An electrolytic treatment that increases the thickness and density of the natural oxide film on aluminium alloy.
notes.explanation: The part is the positive pole in a bath where chromic acid or another oxidising agent produces the naturally protective oxide.
notes.example: Like thickening the skin a metal already grows, rather than painting over it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Anodizing”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: The aluminum alloy sheet or casting is the positive pole in an electrolytic bath in which chromic acid or other oxidizing agent produces an aluminum oxide film on the metal surface. Aluminum oxide is naturally protective. Anodizing merely increases the thickness and density of the natural oxide film.

notes.front: What is alodising (spelt “alodizing” in the handbook)?
notes.back: A simple chemical treatment for all aluminium alloys that increases corrosion resistance and improves paint bonding.
notes.explanation: Its simplicity is why it is rapidly replacing anodising in aircraft work.
notes.example: Like anodising without the electrolytic bath: the chemical is dipped, sprayed or brushed on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Alodizing”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: Alodizing is a simple chemical treatment for all aluminum alloys to increase their corrosion resistance and to improve their paint bonding qualities. Because of its simplicity, it is rapidly replacing anodizing in aircraft work.

notes.front: In aluminium corrosion repair, what is a conversion coating?
notes.back: A chemical coating, such as a chromate conversion coating, applied to bare aluminium immediately after corrosion is removed.
notes.explanation: The circular requires it immediately once the corrosion is gone and the area is well rinsed with clean water.
notes.example: Like Alodine 1200 brushed onto a freshly cleaned aluminium repair.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-136d(2)(e), p. 6-33
notes.evidence: (e) Once the corrosion has been removed and the area well rinsed with clean water, a chromate conversion coating, such as MIL-C-81706 or MIL-C-5541 Alodine 1200, must be applied immediately thereafter.

notes.front: What is chromic acid inhibitor?
notes.back: A 10 percent solution by weight of chromic acid, activated with a little sulfuric acid, for exposed or corroded aluminium.
notes.explanation: It tends to restore the protective oxide coating, and it may also be used on corroded magnesium.
notes.example: Like a tonic brushed onto a scraped aluminium patch to help its protective oxide return.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Chromic Acid Inhibitor”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: A 10 percent solution by weight of chromic acid, activated by a small amount of sulfuric acid, is particularly effective in treating exposed or corroded aluminum surfaces. It may also be used to treat corroded magnesium. This treatment tends to restore the protective oxide coating on the metal surface.

notes.front: What is sodium dichromate solution, as a surface treatment?
notes.back: A less active treatment for aluminium: a solution of sodium dichromate and chromic acid.
notes.explanation: If it is trapped in a joint, it is less likely to corrode metal than chromic acid inhibitor is.
notes.example: Like a milder cousin of the chromic acid wipe.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Sodium Dichromate Solution”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: A less active chemical mixture for surface treatment of aluminum is a solution of sodium dichromate and chromic acid. Entrapped solutions of this mixture are less likely to corrode metal surfaces than chromic acid inhibitor solutions.

notes.front: What role do protective paint finishes play in corrosion control?
notes.back: A good, intact paint finish is the most effective barrier between metal surfaces and corrosive media.
notes.explanation: The commonest are catalysed polyurethane enamel, waterborne polyurethane enamel and two-part epoxy paint.
notes.example: Like the enamel on a bath: while it is unbroken, water never reaches the iron beneath.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Protective Paint Finishes”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: A good, intact paint finish is the most effective barrier between metal surfaces and corrosive media. [Figure 8-31] The most common finishes include catalyzed polyurethane enamel, waterborne polyurethane enamel, and two-part epoxy paint.

notes.front: What is a corrosion preventive compound (CPC)?
notes.back: A compound applied to protect metal against corrosion; examples include waxy sealants and thin-film dielectrics.
notes.explanation: Mechanics are expected to choose the best compound for the job and how often to reapply it.
notes.example: Like the waxy film sprayed inside a car door sill.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant ACS (FAA-S-ACS-1), Area I, Subject G, p. 11
notes.evidence: AM.I.G.K8 Corrosion preventive compounds (CPC) (e.g., waxy sealants, thin-film dielectrics). AM.I.G.K9 Selection of optimal CPC and frequency of treatment.

notes.front: What is methyl ethyl ketone (MEK)?
notes.back: A very active solvent and metal cleaner, also a paint stripper for small areas, with a flashpoint of about 24 °F.
notes.explanation: It is toxic when inhaled, so safety precautions must be observed.
notes.example: Like a strong paint thinner, but far more volatile.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Methyl Ethyl Ketone (MEK)”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: MEK is also available as a solvent cleaner for metal surfaces and paint stripper for small areas. This is a very active solvent and metal cleaner with a flashpoint of about 24 °F. It is toxic when inhaled, and safety precautions must be observed during its use.

notes.front: What is the cleaning compound for oxygen systems?
notes.back: Anhydrous (waterless) ethyl alcohol or isopropyl (anti-icing fluid) alcohol.
notes.explanation: It is for accessible oxygen-system parts such as crew masks and lines.
notes.example: Like wiping a mask with surgical spirit rather than soapy water.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Cleaning Compound for Oxygen Systems”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: Cleaning compounds for use in the oxygen system are anhydrous (waterless) ethyl alcohol or isopropyl (antiicing fluid) alcohol. These may be used to clean accessible components of the oxygen system, such as crew masks and lines.

notes.front: What is an emulsion cleaner?
notes.back: A solvent or water emulsion compound for general aircraft cleaning; solvent emulsions shift heavy carbon, grease, oil or tar.
notes.explanation: Used as instructed, solvent emulsions do not affect good paint coatings or organic finishes.
notes.example: Like a heavy-duty hand cleaner that lifts tar yet leaves the skin alone.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Emulsion Cleaners”, p. 8-28
notes.evidence: Solvent and water emulsion compounds are used in general aircraft cleaning. Solvent emulsions are particularly useful in the removal of heavy deposits, such as carbon, grease, oil, or tar. When used in accordance with instructions, these solvent emulsions do not affect good paint coatings or organic finishes.

notes.front: What is a detergent cleaner, such as aircraft surface cleaning compound?
notes.back: A mild cleaner for light to medium soils, operational films, oils or greases on painted and unpainted aircraft surfaces.
notes.explanation: It is safe on all surfaces, including fabrics, leather and transparent plastics.
notes.example: Like a gentle car shampoo, as opposed to a degreaser.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Soaps & Detergent Cleaners”, p. 8-28
notes.evidence: Specification MIL-C-5410 Type I and II materials are used in general cleaning of painted and unpainted aircraft surfaces for the removal of light to medium soils, operational films, oils, or greases. They are safe to use on all surfaces, including fabrics, leather, and transparent plastics.

notes.front: What is phosphoric-citric acid, as an aircraft cleaner?
notes.back: An acid cleaner for aluminium: Type I is ready to use; Type II is a concentrate diluted with mineral spirits and water.
notes.explanation: Rubber gloves and goggles keep it off the skin.
notes.example: Like a mild descaler, used on bare aluminium.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Phosphoric-citric Acid”, p. 8-29
notes.evidence: A phosphoric-citric acid mixture (Type I) for cleaning aluminum surfaces is available and is ready to use as packaged. Type II is a concentrate that must be diluted with mineral spirits and water. Wear rubber gloves and goggles to avoid skin contact.

notes.front: What is a primer, as a protective coating?
notes.back: An organic coating commonly used to protect metals, such as zinc-chromate primer.
notes.explanation: The circular groups it with enamels and chlorinated rubber compounds as organic coatings.
notes.example: Like the undercoat a decorator puts on bare wood, but chosen to keep corrosion out.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-40, p. 6-15
notes.evidence: 6-40. ORGANIC COATINGS. Zinc-chromate primer, enamels, chlorinated rubber compounds, etc., are organic coatings commonly used to protect metals.

notes.front: What is a topcoat (the circular writes “top coat”)?
notes.back: The finish coat applied over the primer.
notes.explanation: In the circular’s repair steps the primer goes on first and the top coat finish over it, before masking comes off.
notes.example: Like the gloss coat a decorator puts over the undercoat.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-152l, p. 6-40
notes.evidence: l. Apply primer and top coat finish. m. Remove masking and protective coverings.

notes.front: What is an aircraft’s data plate?
notes.back: The fireproof identification plate a manufacturer must attach to each aircraft, carrying the identification data § 45.13 lists.
notes.explanation: The data must be marked on it by an approved fireproof method.
notes.example: Like the chassis plate on a car, but made to survive a fire.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 45 (1 January 2025 edition), § 45.11(a)
notes.evidence: A manufacturer of aircraft covered under § 21.182 of this chapter must mark each aircraft by attaching a fireproof identification plate that— (1) Includes the information specified in § 45.13 using an approved method of fireproof marking;

notes.front: On copper and copper alloys, corrosion forms a {{c1::greenish film}}; on steel it forms reddish rust.
notes.explanation: On aluminium alloys and magnesium it looks different again: pitting and etching, often with a grey or white powdery deposit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: On the surface of aluminum alloys and magnesium, it appears as pitting and etching and is often combined with a gray or white powdery deposit. On copper and copper alloys, the corrosion forms a greenish film; on steel, a reddish corrosion byproduct commonly referred to as rust.

notes.front: An owner says her new aircraft, built mainly of composite, needs no watching for corrosion. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: Composite airframes have not removed the need for careful corrosion monitoring.
notes.explanation: The airframe itself may not corrode, but the metal components and accessories inside it can.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: The introduction of airframes built primarily of composite components has not eliminated the need for careful monitoring of aircraft with regard to corrosion. The airframe itself may not be subject to corrosion; however, the use of metal components and accessories within the airframe means

notes.front: Type of metal is a factor in corrosion: which metals corrode easily and which do not?
notes.back: Active metals such as magnesium and aluminium corrode easily; noble metals such as gold and silver do not.
notes.explanation: The difference is how easily each metal loses electrons.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pure Metals”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: The most active metals (those that lose electrons easily), such as magnesium and aluminum, corrode easily. The most noble metals (those that do not lose electrons easily), such as gold and silver, do not corrode easily.

notes.front: Heat-treatment and grain direction are factors in corrosion. What does heating and cooling in manufacture do to an alloy?
notes.back: It can leave the alloy structure non-uniform.
notes.explanation: That non-uniform structure is what intergranular corrosion attacks, and it may give no visible sign at the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Intergranular Corrosion”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: [Figure 8-14] The lack of uniformity is caused by changes that occur in the alloy during the heating and cooling process of the material’s manufacturing. Intergranular corrosion may exist without visible surface evidence.

notes.front: The presence of a dissimilar, less corrodible metal is a factor in corrosion. What makes the action between two bare metals faster?
notes.back: Salt water as the moisture: it accelerates the electrolytic action.
notes.explanation: Two different bare metals only set up electrolytic action when moisture is present; the result is oxidation of one or both.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Protection of Dissimilar Metal Contacts”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: Contact of different bare metals creates an electrolytic action when moisture is present. If this moisture is salt water, the electrolytic action is accelerated. The result of dissimilar metal contact is oxidation (decomposition) of one or both metals.

notes.front: Anodic and cathodic surface areas are a factor in galvanic corrosion. When is the attack rapid and severe?
notes.back: When the corroding metal’s surface area is smaller than the less active metal’s.
notes.explanation: When the corroding metal is the larger of the two, the attack is slow and superficial instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Galvanic Corrosion”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: The rate of galvanic corrosion also depends on the size of the parts in contact. If the surface area of the corroding metal is smaller than the surface area of the less active metal, corrosion is rapid and severe. When the corroding metal is larger than the less active metal, corrosion is slow and superficial.

notes.front: Temperature is a factor in corrosion. In what kind of climate is electrochemical attack faster?
notes.back: A hot, moist climate.
notes.explanation: Moisture-laden marine air is also considerably more harmful than a dry climate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Climate”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: In a predominately marine environment (with exposure to sea water and salt air), moisture-laden air is considerably more detrimental to an aircraft than it would be if all operations were conducted in a dry climate. Temperature considerations are important, because the speed of electrochemical attack is increased in a hot, moist climate.

notes.front: Among the factors affecting corrosion, the handbook lists the presence of electrolytes such as {{c1::hard water, salt water and battery fluids}}.
notes.explanation: The list is open (“etc.”), and the same list puts temperature just before electrolytes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Factors Affecting Corrosion”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: 5. Temperature 6. Presence of electrolytes (hard water, salt water, battery fluids, etc.)

notes.front: Availability of oxygen is a factor in corrosion. In an oxygen concentration cell, where does the corrosion occur?
notes.back: At the area of low oxygen concentration.
notes.explanation: That area acts as the anode; typical spots are under gaskets, wood, rubber and other materials touching the metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Oxygen Concentration Cells”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: Typical locations of oxygen concentration cells are under gaskets, wood, rubber, and other materials in contact with the metal surface. Corrosion occurs at the area of low oxygen concentration (anode).

notes.front: The presence of biological organisms is a factor in corrosion. How do slimes, moulds and fungi raise the risk?
notes.back: Once established, they keep the area damp.
notes.explanation: They grow on damp surfaces in the first place, some of them too small to see.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Micro-organisms”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Slimes, molds, fungi and other living organisms (some microscopic) can grow on damp surfaces. Once they are established, the area tends to remain damp, increasing the possibility of corrosion.

notes.front: Mechanical stress is a factor in corrosion. What can residual stress from machining, forming, welding or heat-treatment do?
notes.back: Cause cracking in a corrosive environment.
notes.explanation: It happens once the threshold for stress corrosion is exceeded.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Manufacturing Processes”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Manufacturing processes, such as machining, forming, welding, or heat-treatment, can leave stresses in aircraft parts. The residual stress can cause cracking in a corrosive environment when the threshold for stress corrosion is exceeded.

notes.front: Time of exposure is a factor in corrosion. Once the deposits are removed, what decides how etched and pitted the surface looks?
notes.back: The length of exposure and the severity of the attack.
notes.explanation: Longer exposure and a more severe attack leave a more etched and pitted surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: When the gray, white, green, or reddish deposits are removed, each of the surfaces may appear etched and pitted, depending upon the length of exposure and severity of attack.

notes.front: Pencil marks on aircraft metal are listed as a corrosion factor. Why should graphite never touch structural metal?
notes.back: Graphite is cathodic to all structural metals and causes galvanic corrosion when moisture is present.
notes.explanation: The same reason bars graphite as a lubricant on any component.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-91d, p. 6-23
notes.evidence: d. Graphite should not be used as a lubricant for any component. Graphite is cathodic to all structural metals and will generate galvanic corrosion in the presence of moisture, especially if the graphite is applied in dry form.

notes.front: An aircraft is based in a zone rated severe on the corrosion severity map. What interval does the handbook suggest for cleaning, inspection, lubrication and preservation?
notes.back: D: every 15 days.
notes.choices:
A) Every 90 days
B) Every 45 days
C) Every 30 days
D) Every 15 days
notes.choicesExplained: A is the mild-zone interval. B is the moderate-zone interval. C is not a figure the handbook gives.
notes.explanation: The handbook scales the interval to the zone: 90 days for mild, 45 for moderate and 15 for severe.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Geographical Location”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Suggested intervals for cleaning, inspection, lubrication, and preservation when located in mild zones are every 90 days, moderate zones every 45 days, and severe zones every 15 days.

notes.front: What are the most common agents of direct chemical attack on aircraft?
notes.back: Battery acid or fumes; flux residue from poorly cleaned joints; trapped caustic cleaning solutions.
notes.explanation: Each one leaves a caustic agent sitting directly on bare metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Direct Chemical Attack”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: The most common agents causing direct chemical attack on aircraft are: spilled battery acid or fumes from batteries; residual flux deposits resulting from inadequately cleaned, welded, brazed, or soldered joints; and entrapped caustic cleaning solutions.

notes.front: A mechanic has just brazed a small bracket. What should happen to the flux left on the metal?
notes.back: D: remove it immediately after joining.
notes.choices:
A) Leave it; it protects the joint
B) Leave it until it dries, then brush it off
C) Paint over it at the next inspection
D) Remove it immediately after the joining operation
notes.choicesExplained: A and C leave a corrosive, moisture-absorbing residue in place. B delays removal while the residue keeps absorbing moisture.
notes.explanation: Flux residues absorb moisture and, unless carefully removed, tend to cause severe pitting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Direct Chemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: Therefore, it is important to remove residual flux from the metal surface immediately after the joining operation. Flux residues are hygroscopic in nature, absorbing moisture, and unless carefully removed, tend to cause severe pitting.

notes.front: Of the four conditions electrochemical corrosion needs, which one is the anode?
notes.back: A metal subject to corrosion.
notes.explanation: The anode is the member of the cell that is actually eaten away.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: The following four conditions must exist before electrochemical corrosion can occur. [Figure 8-5] 1. A metal subject to corrosion (anode)

notes.front: Of the four conditions electrochemical corrosion needs, what is the cathode?
notes.back: A dissimilar conductive material with less tendency to corrode.
notes.explanation: Its lower tendency to corrode is what makes the other metal the one that corrodes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: 2. A dissimilar conductive material (cathode) that has less tendency to corrode

notes.front: Of the four conditions electrochemical corrosion needs, what is the electrolyte?
notes.back: A continuous, conductive liquid path.
notes.explanation: The path must be both continuous and conductive.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: 3. Presence of a continuous, conductive liquid path (electrolyte)

notes.front: Of the four conditions electrochemical corrosion needs, which one links anode and cathode directly, and in what form is it usually found?
notes.back: Electrical contact between them, usually metal-to-metal contact such as rivets or bolts.
notes.explanation: Removing this or any other one of the four conditions stops the corrosion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: 4. Electrical contact between the anode and the cathode (usually in the form of metal to metal contact, such as rivets, bolts, and corrosion) Elimination of any one of these conditions stops electrochemical corrosion.

notes.front: An aluminium panel with steel fasteners stays free of corrosion while its paint film is unbroken. Which idea explains this?
notes.back: A: removing any one of the four conditions stops it.
notes.choices:
A) Removing any one of the four conditions stops electrochemical corrosion
B) Paint makes the fasteners less noble
C) Paint turns the aluminium into the cathode
D) Paint raises the metal’s endurance limit
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: paint does not change which metal is anodic. D: endurance limit belongs to fatigue, not to this cell.
notes.explanation: Remove any one condition and the corrosion stops; but paint can also mask early corrosion, so painted surfaces are checked often for blisters, flakes, chips and lumps.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electrochemical Attack”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: Elimination of any one of these conditions stops electrochemical corrosion. NOTE: Paint can mask the initial stages of corrosion. Since corrosion products occupy more volume than the original metal, painted surfaces must be inspected often for irregularities, such as blisters, flakes, chips, and lumps.

notes.front: The paint on a wing skin shows small blisters, but there is no powder or roughening. What is the likeliest cause?
notes.back: B: corrosion spreading under the coating.
notes.choices:
A) Normal curing of a new paint film
B) Corrosion spreading under the coating, lifting the paint
C) Fretting between skin and rib
D) Filiform traces crossing on steel
notes.choicesExplained: A is not a corrosion sign the handbook gives. C produces debris and a black ring at rivets. D: filiform traces never cross on steel.
notes.explanation: The corrosion products build up beneath the coating, and their pressure lifts the paint into blisters.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Corrosion”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: Sometimes corrosion spreads under the surface coating and cannot be recognized by either the roughening of the surface or the powdery deposit. Instead, closer inspection reveals the paint or plating is lifted off the surface in small blisters that result from the pressure of the underlying accumulation of corrosion products.

notes.front: Filiform corrosion occurs when relative humidity is between {{c1::78 and 90}} percent and the surface is slightly acidic.
notes.explanation: Polyurethane finishes are especially susceptible to it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Filiform Corrosion”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: Polyurethane finishes are especially susceptible to filiform corrosion. Filiform occurs when the relative humidity of the air is between 78–90 percent, and the surface is slightly acidic.

notes.front: A polyurethane-painted aircraft keeps developing filiform corrosion in its hangar. Which step does the handbook give to prevent it?
notes.back: D: store it below 70 percent relative humidity.
notes.choices:
A) Rinse it with hard water weekly
B) Buff the paint to a high gloss
C) Apply a second coat of the same polyurethane
D) Store it where relative humidity is below 70 percent
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are not measures the handbook gives. A: washing is meant to remove acidic contaminants, and hard water is itself listed as an electrolyte.
notes.explanation: Low humidity, coatings that resist oxygen and water vapour, and washing off acidic contaminants are the three preventives.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Filiform Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Filiform corrosion can be prevented by storing aircraft in an environment with a relative humidity below 70 percent, using coating systems having a low rate of diffusion for oxygen and water vapors, and by washing the aircraft to remove acidic contaminants from the surface,

notes.front: A white, dust-like powder blotches a magnesium fitting. Wiped away, it leaves tiny holes. How should the damage be judged?
notes.back: B: as possibly deep, out of proportion to its look.
notes.choices:
A) As cosmetic, since the holes are tiny
B) As possibly deep: pits can do damage out of proportion to their surface look
C) As fretting, since there is powder
D) As exfoliation, since grains are lifting
notes.choicesExplained: A underrates pitting. C: fretting needs relative motion between mating parts. D: nothing here is lifting grains.
notes.explanation: The small openings may penetrate deeply into structural members.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Pitting Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: It is first noticeable as a white or gray powdery deposit, similar to dust, which blotches the surface. When the deposit is cleaned away, tiny holes or pits can be seen in the surface. These small surface openings may penetrate deeply into structural members and cause damage completely out of proportion to its surface appearance.

notes.front: Why must steel wool or a steel wire brush never be used on aluminium or magnesium?
notes.back: It forces small pieces of steel into the metal, causing corrosion and ruining the adjoining surface.
notes.explanation: This is contamination by mechanical means, which can induce dissimilar metal corrosion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Dissimilar Metal Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: The contamination of a metal’s surface by mechanical means can also induce dissimilar metal corrosion. The improper use of steel cleaning products, such as steel wool or a steel wire brush on aluminum or magnesium, can force small pieces of steel into the metal being cleaned, causing corrosion and ruining the adjoining surface.

notes.front: A fitting joins dissimilar metals and its insulation may have been left out on assembly. Nothing shows on the outside. How can corrosion there be found before the structure fails?
notes.back: A: by disassembly and inspection.
notes.choices:
A) By disassembly and inspection
B) By tapping the fitting and listening
C) By a walk-round glance
D) By checking the paint colour
notes.choicesExplained: C and D see only the outside, where nothing shows. B is not a method the handbook gives for this.
notes.explanation: The attack is often out of sight, which is what makes it so serious.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Dissimilar Metal Corrosion”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: This electrochemical attack can be very serious because, in many instances, the action is taking place out of sight, and the only way to detect it prior to structural failure is by disassembly and inspection.

notes.front: What are the three general types of concentration cell corrosion?
notes.back: Metal ion concentration cells, oxygen concentration cells and active-passive cells.
notes.explanation: Each type is named after what differs between the two areas of the cell.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Concentration Cell Corrosion”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: oxygen concentration cells, and active-passive cells are three general types of concentration cell corrosion.

notes.front: Which high-strength aluminium alloys does the handbook name as more susceptible to intergranular corrosion, and when?
notes.back: 2014 and 7075, if improperly heat-treated and then exposed to a corrosive environment.
notes.explanation: Such corrosion may exist with no visible evidence at the surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Intergranular Corrosion”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: Intergranular corrosion may exist without visible surface evidence. High-strength aluminum alloys, such as 2014 and 7075, are more susceptible to intergranular corrosion if they have been improperly heattreated and then exposed to a corrosive environment.

notes.front: Intergranular corrosion is found in a heat-treated aluminium fitting, and the manufacturer’s limits do not cover the damage. What should happen?
notes.back: C: have the strength loss evaluated, with a designated engineering representative assessing the damage.
notes.choices:
A) Light cleaning only, then paint
B) Remove the visible powder and paint over the layers
C) Evaluate the strength loss, bringing in a designated engineering representative to assess the damage
D) Fill the area with sealant
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D all skip the evaluation of remaining strength that must come before repair or replacement.
notes.explanation: Any loss of structural strength must be evaluated before the part is repaired or replaced.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Intergranular Corrosion in Heat-Treated Aluminum Alloy Surfaces”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: to evaluate the remaining structural strength of the component. Corrosion depth and removal limits have been established for some aircraft. Any loss of structural strength must be evaluated prior to repair or replacement of the part. If the manufacturer’s limits do not adequately address the damage, a designated engineering representative (DER) can be brought in to assess the damage.

notes.front: An extruded spar cap shows surface grains lifting like leaves. Which form of corrosion is this, and which methods help detect it early?
notes.back: A: exfoliation, found early with ultrasonic and eddy current methods.
notes.choices:
A) Exfoliation; ultrasonic and eddy current inspection
B) Filiform; visual check of the paint only
C) Fretting; checking rivets for a black ring
D) Surface corrosion; a flashlight alone
notes.choicesExplained: B: filiform is wormlike traces under paint. C: fretting needs slight motion between mating surfaces. D: surface corrosion does not lift grains.
notes.explanation: It is most often seen on extruded sections, where grains are usually thinner than in rolled forms, and is hard to see at first.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exfoliation Corrosion”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: is most often seen on extruded sections where grain thickness is usually less than in rolled forms. This type of corrosion is difficult to detect in its initial stage. Extruded components, such as spars, can be subject to this type of corrosion. Ultrasonic and eddy current inspection methods are being used with a great deal of success.

notes.front: Which environment causes stress-corrosion cracking of high-strength, heat-treated steel and aluminium alloys, and which one attacks some titanium alloys?
notes.back: Salt solutions and sea water; methyl alcohol-hydrochloric acid solutions for some titanium alloys.
notes.explanation: Magnesium alloys are different again: they may stress-corrode in moist air.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Stress-Corrosion/Cracking”, p. 8-8
notes.evidence: Salt solutions and sea water cause stress corrosion cracking of high-strength, heat-treated steel and aluminum alloys. 2. Methyl alcohol-hydrochloric acid solutions cause stress corrosion cracking of some titanium alloys. 3. Magnesium alloys may stress corrode in moist air.

notes.front: A bolt in a seaplane float fitting was over-torqued at assembly. Which risk does this add?
notes.back: C: trapped internal stress, a setting for stress-corrosion cracking.
notes.choices:
A) Filiform corrosion under the paint
B) Fretting from the bolt head rotating
C) Internal stress that can lead to stress-corrosion cracking
D) Nothing, provided the bolt is painted
notes.choicesExplained: A depends on humidity and an organic coating, not torque. B needs repeated slight motion. D: paint does not remove stress.
notes.explanation: Riveting, welding, bolting, clamping and press fits can all introduce such stress.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Stress-Corrosion/Cracking”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: The stress may be externally introduced in part structure by riveting, welding, bolting, clamping, press fit, etc. If a slight mismatch occurs or a fastener is over-torqued, internal stress

notes.front: What is the most common example of fretting corrosion, and how is it recognised?
notes.back: The smoking rivet on cowlings and wing skins, identified by a black ring around the rivet.
notes.explanation: Unusually, this reaction is not driven by an electrolyte, and moisture may even inhibit it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fretting Corrosion”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: The most common example of fretting corrosion is the smoking rivet found on engine cowling and wing skins. This is one corrosion reaction that is not driven by an electrolyte, and in fact, moisture may inhibit the reaction. A smoking rivet is identified by a black ring around the rivet.

notes.front: A bearing that has sat still under slight vibration shows grooves like pressure indentations. What is this damage called?
notes.back: A: false brinelling, a fretting corrosion.
notes.choices:
A) False brinelling, a fretting corrosion
B) Filiform corrosion
C) Intergranular corrosion
D) Exfoliation
notes.choicesExplained: D lifts grains of extrusions. B is wormlike traces under paint. C attacks grain boundaries, not bearing faces.
notes.explanation: Small, sharp contact areas wear grooves that resemble brinell marks.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fretting Corrosion”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: If the contact areas are small and sharp, deep grooves resembling brinell markings or pressure indentations may be worn in the rubbing surface. As a result, this type of corrosion on bearing surfaces has also been called false brinelling.

notes.front: Two assemblies join the same dissimilar pair. In one, the corroding metal is a small part against a large, less active part; in the other it is the reverse. Which corrodes rapidly and severely?
notes.back: D: the one where the corroding metal is smaller.
notes.choices:
A) Neither, if the metals are dissimilar
B) The one where the corroding metal has the larger area
C) Both corrode equally
D) The one where the corroding metal has the smaller area
notes.choicesExplained: B gives slow, superficial corrosion. C ignores the area effect. A: dissimilar metals in contact with an electrolyte are exactly what galvanic corrosion needs.
notes.explanation: The rate of galvanic corrosion depends on the size of the parts in contact as well as their activity.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Galvanic Corrosion”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: If the surface area of the corroding metal is smaller than the surface area of the less active metal, corrosion is rapid and severe. When the corroding metal is larger than the less active metal, corrosion is slow and superficial.

notes.front: Aluminium alloy 2024 and passive Type 316 stainless steel touch in salt spray. Using the galvanic series shown, which will corrode?
notes.back: A: the aluminium alloy.
notes.choices:
A) The aluminium alloy, which sits nearer the anodic end
B) Neither, both are alloys
C) Both equally
D) The stainless steel
notes.choicesExplained: D: the stainless steel is nearer the cathodic end. B: alloys corrode like any metal. C: the less noble metal is the one attacked.
notes.explanation: Passive Type 316 sits near the cathodic end, among the metals least likely to corrode.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Concentration Cell Corrosion (Figure 8-6)”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Type 316 stainless steel (passive) Hastelloy alloy C (passive) Silver Titanium Graphite Gold Platinum Metal least likely to corrode (cathodic)
