notes.front: Which acids does the handbook call the most destructive to airframe alloys?
notes.back: Sulfuric (battery) acid, halogen acids, nitrous oxide compounds and organic acids in human and animal wastes.
notes.explanation: Even moderately strong acids severely corrode most airframe alloys.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Common Corrosive Agents”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Acids—moderately strong acids severely corrode most of the alloys used in airframes. The most destructive are sulfuric acid (battery acid), halogen acids (hydrochloric, hydrofluoric, and hydrobromic), nitrous oxide compounds, and organic acids found in the wastes of humans and animals.

notes.front: Which alkali are aluminium alloys highly resistant to, unlike washing soda, potash and lime?
notes.back: Ammonia.
notes.explanation: Aluminium alloys are highly resistant to ammonia even though it is an alkali.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Common Corrosive Agents”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Substances particularly corrosive to aluminum are washing soda, potash (wood ashes), and lime (cement dust). Ammonia, an alkali, is an exception because aluminum alloys are highly resistant to it.

notes.front: Why do most salt solutions promote corrosive attack?
notes.back: They are good electrolytes.
notes.explanation: Some stainless-steel alloys resist attack by salt solutions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Common Corrosive Agents”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Salts—most salt solutions are good electrolytes and can promote corrosive attack. Some stainless-steel alloys are resistant to attack by salt solutions but aluminum alloy, magnesium alloys, and other steels are

notes.front: What are the major atmospheric corrosive agents?
notes.back: Oxygen and airborne moisture.
notes.explanation: Extra moisture often speeds the attack, particularly on ferrous alloys.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Common Corrosive Agents”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Atmosphere—the major atmospheric corrosive agents are oxygen and airborne moisture. Corrosion often results from the direct action of atmospheric oxygen and moisture on metal, and the presence of additional moisture often accelerates corrosive attack, particularly on ferrous alloys.

notes.front: Which characteristic of water helps decide how corrosive it is?
notes.back: Its conductivity: its ability to act as an electrolyte and conduct a current.
notes.explanation: Dissolved minerals, organic impurities and gases, especially oxygen, also set its corrosiveness.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Common Corrosive Agents”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Water—the corrosiveness of water depends on the type and quantity of dissolved mineral and organic impurities and dissolved gasses (particularly oxygen) in the water. One characteristic of water that determines its corrosiveness is the conductivity or ability to act as an electrolyte and conduct a current.

notes.front: An aircraft parked beside a building site is coated in cement dust. Which is true of this deposit on aluminium?
notes.back: C: lime (cement dust) is particularly corrosive to aluminium.
notes.choices:
A) It protects the skin like a conversion coating
B) It is harmless, as alkalies do not attack aluminium
C) Lime (cement dust) is particularly corrosive to aluminium
D) It matters only on steel
notes.choicesExplained: B: aluminium is prone to attack by many alkaline solutions. A: dust is not a treatment. D: the handbook names aluminium specifically.
notes.explanation: Aluminium and magnesium alloys are exceedingly prone to attack by alkaline solutions without an inhibitor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Common Corrosive Agents”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Aluminum and magnesium alloys are exceedingly prone to corrosive attack by many alkaline solutions unless the solutions contain a corrosion inhibitor. Substances particularly corrosive to aluminum are washing soda, potash (wood ashes), and lime (cement dust).

notes.front: During any corrosion control maintenance, what should be consulted about the chemicals used?
notes.back: The Safety Data Sheet for each chemical.
notes.explanation: Corrosion control is continuous preventive maintenance, and every chemical in it has its own hazards.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Preventive Maintenance”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: In spite of these improvements, corrosion and its control is a very real problem that requires continuous preventive maintenance. During any corrosion control maintenance, consult the Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for information on any chemicals used in the process.

notes.front: Which two corrosion preventive tasks does the handbook list as daily?
notes.back: Draining fuel cell sumps and wiping down exposed critical areas.
notes.explanation: They sit in the handbook’s list of preventive functions next to keeping drain holes free of obstructions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Preventive Maintenance”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: 8. Keeping drain holes free of obstructions 9. Daily draining of fuel cell sumps 10. Daily wipe down of exposed critical areas

notes.front: A leased aircraft returns after a year in which no regular corrosion preventive maintenance was done. What should the new operator expect?
notes.back: C: usually quite a lot of maintenance.
notes.choices:
A) Little extra work, as corrosion is slow
B) Only a wash
C) Usually quite a lot of maintenance to repair built-up corrosion
D) Nothing, if the paint looks good
notes.choicesExplained: A and B understate it. D: paint can mask the early stages of corrosion.
notes.explanation: Damage accumulates while the programme lapses, and bringing the aircraft back to standard takes work.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Preventive Maintenance”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: After any period where regular corrosion preventive maintenance is interrupted, the amount of maintenance required to repair accumulated corrosion damage and bring the aircraft back up to standard is usually quite high.

notes.front: How does every corrosion inspection begin, and what tools does the general visual inspection use?
notes.back: With thorough cleaning; then a flashlight, inspection mirror and a 5 to 10 power magnifying glass.
notes.explanation: The general inspection looks for obvious defects and suspect areas, which a detailed inspection then examines.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Inspection”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: All corrosion inspections start with a thorough cleaning of the area to be inspected. A general visual inspection of the area follows using a flashlight, inspection mirror, and a 5– l0X magnifying glass.

notes.front: In bilge areas, how can a hidden chemical cell form?
notes.back: Residual oil masks small amounts of water that settle to the bottom.
notes.explanation: Bilges are natural collection points for waste fluids, water, dirt and debris.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Bilge Areas”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: These are natural collection points for waste hydraulic fluids, water, dirt, and odds and ends of debris. Residual oil quite often masks small quantities of water that settle to the bottom and set up a hidden chemical cell.

notes.front: Around lavatories and galleys, how can contaminants that are not corrosive themselves still cause corrosion?
notes.back: They attract and hold moisture.
notes.explanation: Spilled food and waste collect behind lavatories, sinks and ranges if not kept clean.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Lavatories, Buffets, & Galleys”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: Even if some contaminants are not corrosive in themselves, they attract and retain moisture and, in turn, cause corrosive attack. Pay attention to bilge areas located under galleys and lavatories.

notes.front: In the wheel well, why can a partly applied preservative be worse than it looks?
notes.back: It tends to mask corrosion rather than prevent it.
notes.explanation: Complicated shapes make full paint coverage hard to achieve and keep.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Wheel Well and Landing Gear”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: Because of the many complicated shapes, assemblies, and fittings, complete area paint film coverage is difficult to attain and maintain. A partially applied preservative tends to mask corrosion rather than prevent it.

notes.front: What inspection of water entrapment areas is a standard daily requirement, and why?
notes.back: Low point drains, which debris, grease or sealant can block.
notes.explanation: Drains are fitted wherever water may collect, by design requirement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Water Entrapment Areas”, p. 8-12
notes.evidence: Design specifications require that aircraft have drains installed in all areas where water may collect. Daily inspection of low point drains is a standard requirement. If this inspection is neglected, the drains may become ineffective because of accumulated debris, grease, or sealants.

notes.front: Why are engine frontal areas and cooling air vents prone to corrosion?
notes.back: Dirt, gravel and rain erosion wear away the protective finish.
notes.explanation: Parts such as cylinder fins may be left unpainted for heat dissipation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Engine Frontal Areas & Cooling Air Vents”, p. 8-13
notes.evidence: These areas are being constantly abraded with airborne dirt and dust, bits of gravel from runways, and rain erosion, leading to removal of the protective finish. Furthermore, cores of radiator coolers, reciprocating engine cylinder fins, etc., may not be painted due to the requirement for heat dissipation.

notes.front: How should wing flap and spoiler recesses be inspected for corrosion?
notes.back: With the flaps and spoilers fully deployed.
notes.explanation: Normally retracted, the recesses can collect dirt and water unnoticed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Wing Flap & Spoiler Recesses”, p. 8-13
notes.evidence: Dirt and water may collect in flap and spoiler recesses unnoticed, because they are normally retracted. For this reason, these recesses are potential corrosion problem areas. Inspect these areas with the spoilers and flaps in the fully deployed position.

notes.front: Why are piano-type hinges prime spots for corrosion, and what should be used when servicing them?
notes.back: The steel pin contacts the aluminium hinge; use water-displacing lubricants.
notes.explanation: Inspection includes lubricating and cycling the hinge so the lubricant penetrates fully.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Miscellaneous Trouble Areas”, p. 8-13
notes.evidence: Piano-type hinges are prime spots for corrosion due to the dissimilar metal contact between the steel pin and aluminum hinge. They are also natural traps for dirt, salt, and moisture. Inspection of hinges must include lubrication and actuation through several cycles to ensure complete lubricant penetration. Use water-displacing lubricants when servicing piano hinges.

notes.front: A control cable shows external corrosion. With tension relieved, what must be checked, and what happens if it is found?
notes.back: Internal corrosion; a cable with internal corrosion is replaced.
notes.explanation: Light external corrosion can be removed; internal corrosion cannot be tolerated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Miscellaneous Trouble Areas”, p. 8-14
notes.evidence: and check the cable for internal corrosion. Replace cables that have internal corrosion. Remove light external corrosion with a nonwoven abrasive pad lightly soaked in oil or, alternatively, a steel wire brush.

notes.front: A mechanic is planning which areas to clean, inspect and treat more often than the rest. What does the handbook say about its own list of corrosion-prone areas?
notes.back: C: it is not necessarily complete; use the maintenance manual too.
notes.choices:
A) It is complete for every aircraft
B) It replaces the maintenance manual
C) It is not necessarily complete; the model’s maintenance manual may expand it
D) It applies only to seaplanes
notes.choicesExplained: A and B overstate it. D: the list covers problem areas common to all aircraft.
notes.explanation: Each model has its own special characteristics that its maintenance manual covers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion Prone Areas”, p. 8-11
notes.evidence: These areas should be cleaned, inspected, and treated more frequently than less corrosion prone areas. This information is not necessarily complete and may be amplified and expanded to cover the special characteristics of the particular aircraft model involved by referring to the applicable maintenance manual.

notes.front: During a visual inspection of external skin, what may bulging of the skin at lap joints indicate?
notes.back: Corrosion between the faying surfaces.
notes.explanation: Corrosion products build up where the surfaces meet, pushing the skin out.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-69c, p. 6-19
notes.evidence: c. Inspect lap joints for bulging of skin surface, which may indicate the presence of corrosion between the faying surfaces.

notes.front: Why does the circular classify corrosion by physical appearance?
notes.back: All corrosive attacks begin on the metal surface.
notes.explanation: Since every attack starts on the surface, appearance is a convenient way to identify the form.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-11, p. 6-5
notes.evidence: 6-11. GENERAL. All corrosive attacks begin on the surface of the metal, making the classification of corrosion by physical appearance a convenient means of identification.

notes.front: In general, what does a complete corrosion treatment involve?
notes.back: Clean and strip, remove corrosion products, neutralise residues, restore protective films, then coat or paint.
notes.explanation: The treatment ends by restoring protective films and applying temporary or permanent coatings or paint.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion Removal”, p. 8-14
notes.evidence: In general, any complete corrosion treatment involves cleaning and stripping of the corroded area, removing as much of the corrosion products as practicable, neutralizing any residual materials remaining in pits and crevices, restoring protective surface films, and applying temporary or permanent coatings or paint finishes.

notes.front: Corrosion damage on a fitting is severe and exceeds the damage limits the manufacturer sets. What must happen?
notes.back: B: replace the part.
notes.choices:
A) Blend it deeper
B) Replace the part
C) Treat it with chromic acid and paint
D) Log it and recheck next year
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are for damage within limits. D leaves damaged structure in service.
notes.explanation: Repair means removing all corrosion; beyond the limits, repair is no longer the answer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion Removal”, p. 8-14
notes.evidence: Repair of corrosion damage includes removal of all corrosion and corrosion products. When the corrosion damage is severe and exceeds the damage limits set by the aircraft or parts manufacturer, the part must be replaced.

notes.front: How long is paint stripper left on the surface?
notes.back: Long enough to wrinkle and lift the paint: from 10 minutes to several hours.
notes.explanation: Temperature, humidity and the paint’s condition decide the time.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cleaning and Paint Removal”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: Allow the stripper to remain on the surface for a sufficient length of time to wrinkle and lift the paint. This may be from 10 minutes to several hours, depending on temperature, humidity, and the condition of the paint coat being removed.

notes.front: Which surfaces must be protected from paint remover, and why take care near seam sealants?
notes.back: Synthetic rubber (including tyres), fabric and acrylics; stripper softens gas- and watertight seam sealants.
notes.explanation: Stripper softens and destroys the integrity of those sealants.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cleaning and Paint Removal”, p. 8-14
notes.evidence: Synthetic rubber surfaces, including aircraft tires, fabric, and acrylics, must be thoroughly protected against possible contact with paint remover. Care must be exercised in using paint remover, especially around gas or watertight seam sealants, since the stripper tends to soften and destroy the integrity of these sealants.

notes.front: After a second coat of stripper, paint still clings in a few spots. What may be used to help remove it?
notes.back: C: a nonmetallic scraper.
notes.choices:
A) A steel putty knife
B) A carborundum disc
C) A nonmetallic scraper
D) A steel wire brush
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: only nonmetallic scrapers are to be used. B is not a paint-removal tool the handbook gives.
notes.explanation: Stripper is reapplied where paint stays tightly adhered, and only nonmetallic scrapers are to help remove persistent finishes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cleaning and Paint Removal”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: Reapply the stripper as necessary in areas where the paint remains tightly adhered or where the stripper has dried, and repeat the above process. Only nonmetallic scrapers are to be used to assist in removing persistent paint finishes.

notes.front: Which way must the major axis of a blended dish-out run on a wing, a fuselage and a vertical stabiliser?
notes.back: Spanwise on wings, longitudinally on fuselages, vertically on vertical stabilisers.
notes.explanation: Every dish-out must be elliptical, with its long axis set by the structure it is on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fairing or Blending Reworked Areas”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: All dish-outs must be elliptically shaped with the major axis running spanwise on wings and horizontal stabilizers, longitudinally on fuselages, and vertically on vertical stabilizers.

notes.front: Rework depressions are blended into smooth dish-outs at a length-to-depth ratio of {{c1::20:1}}.
notes.explanation: The dish-outs must be smoothly blended, and the ratio is length to depth.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fairing or Blending Reworked Areas”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: Rework depressions by forming smoothly blended dish-outs, using a ratio of 20:1, length to depth.

notes.front: After corrosion removal, small pits remain in a highly stressed wing fitting. Nearby, a non-critical fairing that was abrasive-blasted also has pits. What should be done?
notes.back: A: blend the fitting; the fairing’s pits may stay.
notes.choices:
A) Blend out the fitting’s pits; leaving the fairing’s is acceptable
B) Leave both
C) Blend out the fairing only
D) Blend out both
notes.choicesExplained: D removes metal needlessly on the fairing. B leaves stress risers in critical structure. C has it backwards.
notes.explanation: Pits in critical areas are stress risers that may cause stress-corrosion cracking; on non-critical structure, blending them only removes metal needlessly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fairing or Blending Reworked Areas”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: In critical and highly stressed areas, all pits remaining after the removal of corrosion products must be blended out to prevent stress risers that may cause stress corrosion cracking. [Figure 8-23] On a noncritical structure, it is not necessary to blend out pits remaining after removal of corrosion products by abrasive blasting, since this results in unnecessary metal removal.

notes.front: Why must all rust be removed from steel surfaces?
notes.back: Rust promotes further attack: it attracts moisture and acts as a catalyst for more corrosion.
notes.explanation: Unlike some metal oxides, rust gives the base metal no protection at all.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion of Ferrous Metals”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: Some metal-oxides protect the underlying base metal, but rust is not a protective coating in any sense of the word. Its presence actually promotes additional attack by attracting moisture from the air and acting as a catalyst for additional corrosion.

notes.front: A steel bracket was cleaned of rust with abrasive paper alone. What should the mechanic expect?
notes.back: B: it usually corrodes again more easily.
notes.choices:
A) It will never rust again
B) Residual rust usually stays in small pits, so it usually corrodes again more easily
C) It will rust only if painted
D) It must be scrapped
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the residual rust left in pits. C has no basis in the handbook. D: nothing here says the part must be scrapped.
notes.explanation: Abrasives alone can practically never remove all corrosion products from pits and crevices.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Mechanical Removal of Iron Rust”, p. 8-16
notes.evidence: usually remains in the bottom of small pits and other crevices. It is practically impossible to remove all corrosion products by abrasive or polishing methods alone. As a result, once a part cleaned in such a manner has rusted, it usually corrodes again more easily than it did the first time.

notes.front: Before chemical rust removal, where should the steel part be, if at all possible, and why?
notes.back: Off the airframe, because removing all residue in place can be nearly impossible.
notes.explanation: Caustic products also need the part isolated from nonferrous metals during treatment.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Chemical Removal of Rust”, p. 8-16
notes.evidence: If at all possible, the steel part is removed from the airframe for treatment, as it can be nearly impossible to remove all residue. The use of any caustic rust removal product requires the isolation of the part from any nonferrous metals during treatment

notes.front: Which abrasives are used to remove corrosion from highly stressed steel parts?
notes.back: Mild abrasive papers such as rouge or fine aluminium oxide, fine buffing compounds on cloth wheels, or nonwoven pads.
notes.explanation: The surface must not be overheated while buffing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Removal of Corrosion from Highly Stressed Steel Parts”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: Corrosion products must be removed by careful processing, using mild abrasive papers, such as rouge or fine grit aluminum oxide or fine buffing compounds on cloth buffing wheels. Nonwoven abrasive pads can also be used. It is essential that steel surfaces not be overheated during buffing.

notes.front: A mechanic wants to use a chemical corrosion remover on a high-strength steel landing gear part. What does the handbook require?
notes.back: A: engineering authorisation, because of hydrogen embrittlement.
notes.choices:
A) Engineering authorisation, because such parts are subject to hydrogen embrittlement
B) Nothing special
C) Only a rinse afterwards
D) A steel wire brush first
notes.choicesExplained: B and C ignore the prohibition. D is not the removal method the handbook gives for these parts.
notes.explanation: High-strength steel parts are subject to hydrogen embrittlement.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Removal of Corrosion from Highly Stressed Steel Parts”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: The use of chemical corrosion removers is prohibited without engineering authorization, because high-strength steel parts are subject to hydrogen embrittlement.

notes.front: How thick is the smooth surface oxidation that aluminium alloys commonly form, and is it harmful?
notes.back: From 0.001 to 0.0025 inch thick; it is not considered detrimental.
notes.explanation: It forms a hard-shell barrier against corrosive elements.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion of Aluminum & Aluminum Alloys”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: NOTE: Aluminum alloys commonly form a smooth surface oxidation that is from 0.001" to 0.0025" thick. This is not considered detrimental. The coating provides a hard-shell barrier to the introduction of corrosive elements.

notes.front: Which three forms of attack on aluminium alloys does the handbook call particularly serious?
notes.back: Pits through tubing walls; stress-corrosion cracking under sustained stress; intergranular corrosion in improperly heat-treated alloys.
notes.explanation: The handbook says “at least” three, so other forms can also be serious.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion of Aluminum & Aluminum Alloys”, p. 8-17
notes.evidence: At least three forms of attack on aluminum alloys are particularly serious: the penetrating pit-type corrosion through the walls of aluminum tubing, stress-corrosion cracking of materials under sustained stress, and intergranular corrosion, which is characteristic of certain improperly heattreated aluminum alloys.

notes.front: When cleaning unpainted Alclad, what matters most for protection?
notes.back: Avoid needlessly removing the Alclad layer and exposing the more susceptible alloy beneath.
notes.explanation: Exposing the base alloy is the concern, since it is more susceptible than the Alclad layer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Unpainted Aluminum Surfaces”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: More important from a protection standpoint, avoid unnecessary mechanical removal of the protective Alclad layer and the exposure of the more susceptible aluminum alloy base material.

notes.front: After surface treatment of aluminium that is to be painted, when must the paint coatings be restored?
notes.back: Immediately; the treatment must be done or redone on the same day as the painting.
notes.explanation: If painting slips to another day, the corrosion treatment is reapplied that day.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Unpainted Aluminum Surfaces”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: Restoration of paint coatings must immediately follow any surface treatment performed. In any case, make sure that corrosion treatment is accomplished or is reapplied on the same day that paint refinishing is scheduled.

notes.front: A mechanic has metal polish made for clad aluminium skins and wants to use it on an anodised fitting. Should they?
notes.back: C: no, it would remove the protective anodised film.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it works on any aluminium
B) Yes, but only by machine
C) No: it is abrasive enough to remove the anodised film
D) Only after stripping the paint
notes.choicesExplained: A and B ignore the damage to the film. D does not change what the polish does to the oxide.
notes.explanation: Polish meant for clad skins is abrasive enough to remove the protective anodised film.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Unpainted Aluminum Surfaces”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: Metal polish intended for use on clad aluminum aircraft surfaces must not be used on anodized aluminum, since it is abrasive enough to actually remove the protective anodized film.

notes.front: Why is magnesium corrosion probably the easiest to detect early, and what are its first signs?
notes.back: Its products take up several times the metal’s volume; the paint lifts and white spots appear.
notes.explanation: The white spots rapidly develop into snow-like mounds or even white whiskers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion of Magnesium Alloys”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: Magnesium attack is probably the easiest type of corrosion to detect in its early stages, since magnesium corrosion products occupy several times the volume of the original magnesium metal destroyed. The beginning of attack shows as a lifting of the paint film and white spots on the magnesium surface. These rapidly develop into snow-like mounds or even “white whiskers.”

notes.front: What tools are used to remove corrosion products from magnesium?
notes.back: Stiff hog-bristle brushes and similar nonmetallic tools, including nonwoven abrasive pads.
notes.explanation: The limit to nonmetallic tools applies particularly when treatment is done under field conditions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Wrought Magnesium Sheet & Forgings”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: Limit such mechanical cleaning to the use of stiff, hog bristle brushes and similar nonmetallic cleaning tools (including nonwoven abrasive pads), particularly if treatment is to be performed under field conditions.

notes.front: A mechanic has brushed chromic acid solution into corroded magnesium skin. What comes next?
notes.back: D: leave 5 to 20 minutes, then wipe off the excess.
notes.choices:
A) Let it dry on the surface overnight
B) Paint over it while wet
C) Rinse at once with high-pressure water
D) Leave it 5 to 20 minutes, then wipe off the excess with a clean, damp cloth
notes.choicesExplained: A: dried deposits cause the paint to lift. C removes it before it can act. B: paint goes on once the surface is dry.
notes.explanation: Dried deposits of the solution cause the paint to lift.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Wrought Magnesium Sheet & Forgings”, p. 8-19
notes.evidence: Allow the chromic acid to remain in place for 5 to 20 minutes before wiping up the excess with a clean, damp cloth. Do not allow the excess solution to dry and remain on the surface, as paint lifting is caused by such deposits.

notes.front: Which cleaning tools are prohibited on titanium, and why?
notes.back: Steel wool, iron scrapers and steel brushes, because metal impurities can cause deterioration.
notes.explanation: Metal impurities can make titanium deteriorate, particularly at high temperatures.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Titanium & Titanium Alloys”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: Titanium is, by nature, highly corrosion resistant, but it may show deterioration from the presence of salt deposits and metal impurities, particularly at high temperatures. Therefore, the use of steel wool, iron scrapers, or steel brushes for cleaning or for the removal of corrosion from titanium parts is prohibited.

notes.front: What materials can separate dissimilar metals in a joint?
notes.back: Metal primer, aluminium tape, washers, grease or sealant.
notes.explanation: Which one is used depends on the metals involved.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Protection of Dissimilar Metal Contacts”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: The chart shown in Figure 8-30 lists the metal combinations requiring a protective separator. The separating materials may be metal primer, aluminum tape, washers, grease, or sealant, depending on the metals involved.

notes.front: How are dissimilar metal joints not involving magnesium protected?
notes.back: At least two extra coats of zinc chromate or, preferably, epoxy primer, air-dried 6 hours between coats.
notes.explanation: Epoxy primer is preferred to zinc chromate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Contacts Not Involving Magnesium”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: All dissimilar joints not involving magnesium are protected by the application of a minimum of two coats of zinc chromate or, preferably, epoxy primer in addition to normal primer requirements. Primer is applied by brush or spray and allowed to air dry 6 hours between coats.

notes.front: A magnesium part will bolt to a steel bracket that runs at about 300 °F. How is the joint insulated?
notes.back: C: at least three primer coats, no tape.
notes.choices:
A) Two primer coats plus vinyl tape
B) No insulation, as the heat drives off moisture
C) At least three coats of primer, with no tape
D) Grease only
notes.choicesExplained: A: tape is dropped when service temperatures above 250 °F are expected. B has no basis. D is not the magnesium procedure.
notes.explanation: Tape is dropped when it interferes with assembly, when parts move relative to each other, or when service above 250 °F is expected.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Contacts Involving Magnesium”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: When the thickness of the tape interferes with the assembly of parts, where relative motion exists between parts or when service temperatures above 250 °F are anticipated, the use of tape is eliminated and extra coats (minimum of three) of primer are applied.

notes.front: Does “negligible” corrosion damage mean nothing need be done?
notes.back: No: the corroded surface must still be cleaned, treated and painted as appropriate.
notes.explanation: Negligible damage has generally already scarred or eaten away the protective coats and begun to etch the metal.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion Limits”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: The term “negligible” does not imply that little or nothing is to be done. The corroded surface must be cleaned, treated, and painted as appropriate. Negligible damage, generally, is corrosion that has scarred or eaten away the surface protective coats and begun to etch the metal.

notes.front: Corrosion damage on a skin panel goes beyond negligible but can be fixed by fitting a patch. How is it classed and what governs the repair?
notes.back: B: repairable by patching, repaired per the structural repair manual.
notes.choices:
A) Negligible; clean and paint only
B) Repairable by patching; repair per the structural repair manual
C) Not damage, since it is only corrosion
D) Damage necessitating replacement
notes.choicesExplained: A understates damage beyond negligible. D applies only when repair is not possible. C: the handbook classes corrosion as damage.
notes.explanation: Beyond the repairable classes, when repair is not possible, the component or structure must be replaced.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Corrosion Limits”, p. 8-21
notes.evidence: extending to classifications of “repairable by patching” and “repairable by insertion” must be repaired in accordance with the applicable structural repair manual. When corrosion damage exceeds the damage limits to the extent that repair is not possible, the component or structure must be replaced.

notes.front: Why is chemical cleaning preferred over mechanical cleaning when preparing a surface?
notes.back: Chemical cleaning removes none of the base metal.
notes.explanation: Which chemical process is used depends on the material and on what is being removed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Preparation”, p. 8-21
notes.evidence: Chemical cleaning is preferred over mechanical since none of the base metal is removed by cleaning. There are various chemical processes now in use, and the type used depends on the material being cleaned and the type of foreign matter being removed.

notes.front: A shop proposes blast cleaning a thin Alclad panel with steel grit. What is wrong?
notes.back: B: blasting is not for thin Alclad, and steel grit is not for aluminium.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing
B) Blast cleaning is not for thin aluminium sheet, especially Alclad, and steel grit is not used on aluminium
C) Only the grit size
D) It must be done wet
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D all miss both restrictions.
notes.explanation: The handbook rules out both the method and the medium for this panel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Preparation”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: Blast cleaning, using abrasive media, is not applicable to thin aluminum sheets, particularly Alclad. Steel grits are not used on aluminum or corrosion resistant metals.

notes.front: When repairing an aircraft, what corrosion proofing should be applied?
notes.back: The same type as, or equivalent to, the original, with more if the repair raises susceptibility.
notes.explanation: If the repair itself makes the area more susceptible, extra measures are added.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-29, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: 6-29. GENERAL. In the repair of aircraft, apply corrosion proofing of the same type or equivalent to that originally applied unless the repair would result in increased susceptibility to corrosion, in which case use additional corrosion protection measures.

notes.front: Why must the anodised coating be removed where a bonding wire is attached?
notes.back: It is a poor conductor of electricity.
notes.explanation: Only parts that require bonding lose the coating, and only at the attachment point.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Anodizing”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: The anodic coating is a poor conductor of electricity; therefore, if parts require bonding, the coating is removed where the bonding wire is to be attached.

notes.front: Which tool is approved for cleaning corrosion from an anodised surface?
notes.back: B: a fine-grade nonwoven abrasive pad.
notes.choices:
A) A steel wire brush
B) A fine-grade nonwoven abrasive pad
C) Steel wool
D) A buffing wheel producing a bright finish
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are prohibited on any aluminium. D: producing a buffed finish is prohibited.
notes.explanation: Steel wool, steel wire brushes and harsh abrasives are prohibited on any aluminium surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Anodizing”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: Aluminum wool, nylon webbing impregnated with aluminum oxide abrasive, fine grade, nonwoven abrasive pads, or fiber bristle brushes are the approved tools for cleaning anodized surfaces. The use of steel wool, steel wire brushes, or harsh abrasive materials on any aluminum surface is prohibited.

notes.front: What colour is an alodised coating?
notes.back: From light bluish green on copper-free alloys to olive green on copper-bearing alloys.
notes.explanation: The copper content of the alloy changes the colour.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Alodizing”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: A thin, hard coating results, ranging in color from light, bluish green with a slight iridescence on copper free alloys to an olive green on copper bearing alloys.

notes.front: In alodising, the parts have just been precleaned with an acidic or alkaline cleaner. What is the next step?
notes.back: C: rinse under pressure for 10 to 15 seconds.
notes.choices:
A) Dry in an oven
B) Apply Bonderite at once
C) Rinse with fresh water under pressure for 10 to 15 seconds
D) Dip in a Deoxylyte bath
notes.choicesExplained: B comes after the rinse. A is not a step given. D comes last, after the Bonderite rinse.
notes.explanation: Bonderite goes on only after thorough rinsing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Alodizing”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: The process consists of precleaning with an acidic or alkaline metal cleaner that is applied by either dipping or spraying. The parts are then rinsed with fresh water under pressure for 10 to 15 seconds. After thorough rinsing, Bonderite® is applied by dipping, spraying, or brushing.

notes.front: If primer has not been applied within how many hours of a conversion coating, must the coating be reapplied?
notes.back: 48 hours or more.
notes.explanation: The coating goes on immediately after rework and must be fresh when primer follows.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-136j, p. 6-34
notes.evidence: j. Apply chemical conversion coating, MIL-C-81706, immediately after reworking. If 48 hours or more have elapsed since the conversion coating was first applied and the primer or final paint system has not yet been applied, then reapply the conversion coating before continuing.

notes.front: An aluminium repair beside a magnesium casting and a 180,000 psi steel fitting needs its conversion coating. What precaution applies?
notes.back: B: keep it off the magnesium and high-strength steel.
notes.choices:
A) None, the solution is harmless
B) Keep the solution off the magnesium and the high-strength steel
C) Apply it to all three metals
D) Dilute it with paint thinner
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the circular’s note. D: the solution must not contact paint thinner, as fire may result.
notes.explanation: Contact with thinner, acetone or other combustibles may also start a fire.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-136j, p. 6-34
notes.evidence: NOTE: These solutions should not be allowed to come in contact with magnesium or high-strength steels (180,000 psi). Do not permit solutions or materials to contact paint thinner, acetone, or other combustible material; fire may result.

notes.front: Why have waterborne paint systems grown in popularity?
notes.back: New regulations limit emissions of volatile organic compounds.
notes.explanation: Nitrate and butyrate dope finishes remain available for fabric-covered aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Protective Paint Finishes”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: As new regulations regarding the emission of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are put into effect, the use of waterborne paint systems have increased in popularity. Also, still available are nitrate and butyrate dope finishes for fabric-covered aircraft.

notes.front: Which is the most effective barrier between an aluminium skin and corrosive media?
notes.back: A: a good, intact paint finish.
notes.choices:
A) A good, intact paint finish
B) Frequent washing
C) A coat of wax alone
D) A layer of oil
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D all help in places, but the handbook names an intact paint finish as the most effective barrier.
notes.explanation: The key word is intact: the barrier only works while the film is unbroken.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Protective Paint Finishes”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: A good, intact paint finish is the most effective barrier between metal surfaces and corrosive media.

notes.front: After an aircraft operating over salt water is washed with fresh water and dried, what goes on the propeller and unpainted engine parts?
notes.back: A grade 4 corrosion preventive compound, sprayed or rubbed on lightly.
notes.explanation: It covers the propeller, hubs, blades and other unpainted or unprotected engine and installation parts.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-51a, p. 6-17
notes.evidence: (1) After drying, coat the propeller, hubs, blades, and other unpainted or unprotected parts of the engine and its installation parts by spraying or rubbing lightly with corrosion-preventive compound, Specification MIL-C-16173, Grade 4.

notes.front: While applying corrosion preventive compound to a seaplane engine, a mechanic gets some on the exhaust collector ring. Why should it be wiped off?
notes.back: D: it could be a fire hazard at engine start.
notes.choices:
A) It stains the paint
B) It blocks the drain holes
C) It speeds up exhaust corrosion
D) It could be a fire hazard when the engine starts
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and B are not the reason the circular gives.
notes.explanation: Ignition wires, the anti-icer hose, tyres and other rubber parts are also kept free of it.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-51a(3), p. 6-17
notes.evidence: (3) Wipe off excess mixture. When applying the mixture, take care that as little as possible is deposited on exhaust pipes or collector rings to avoid a fire hazard when the engine is started. Keep the ignition wires, propeller anti-icer feed hose, tires, and other rubber parts free of the mixture.

notes.front: What are the three methods of cleaning an aircraft exterior?
notes.back: Wet wash, dry wash and polishing.
notes.explanation: Polishing itself divides into hand and mechanical polishing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exterior Cleaning”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: There are three methods of cleaning the aircraft exterior: wet wash, dry wash, and polishing. Polishing can be further broken down into hand polishing and mechanical polishing.

notes.front: Which deposits is the dry wash method not suitable for removing?
notes.back: Heavy deposits of carbon, grease or oil, especially in engine exhaust areas.
notes.explanation: Dry wash is for airport film, dust and light dirt when liquids are neither desirable nor practical.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exterior Cleaning”, p. 8-24
notes.evidence: Dry wash is used to remove airport film, dust, and small accumulations of dirt and soil when the use of liquids is neither desirable nor practical. This method is not suitable for removing heavy deposits of carbon, grease, or oil, especially in the engine exhaust areas.

notes.front: Why should an aircraft be washed in the shade whenever possible?
notes.back: Cleaning compounds tend to streak if applied to hot metal or left to dry.
notes.explanation: Covers also go over every opening where water or cleaner might get in and cause damage.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exterior Cleaning”, p. 8-24
notes.evidence: The washing of aircraft should be performed in the shade whenever possible, as cleaning compounds tend to streak the surface if applied to hot metal or are permitted to dry on the area. Install covers over all openings where water or cleaners might enter and cause damage.

notes.front: A dusty acrylic windshield needs cleaning. Which approach does the handbook give?
notes.back: A: flush with fresh water, then wash by hand with soap and water.
notes.choices:
A) Flush with fresh water, then wash with soap and water by hand
B) Wipe it with acetone
C) Rub it with a dry cloth
D) Use a window cleaning spray
notes.choicesExplained: C scratches and builds a static charge that attracts dust. B and D soften plastic and cause crazing.
notes.explanation: Flushing first dissolves salt and carries dust away before anything rubs the soft surface.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Exterior Cleaning”, p. 8-24
notes.evidence: Before applying soap and water to plastic surfaces, flush the plastic surfaces with fresh water to dissolve salt deposits and wash away dust particles. Plastic surfaces are to be washed with soap and water, preferably by hand.

notes.front: Which cleaners are light-duty and which are heavy-duty?
notes.back: Soaps and synthetic detergents are light-duty; solvents and emulsion cleaners are heavy-duty.
notes.explanation: Nontoxic, nonflammable light-duty cleaners are to be used whenever possible.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Aircraft Cleaning”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: The soap and synthetic detergent-type cleaners are used for light-duty cleaning, while the solvent and emulsion-type cleaners are used for heavy-duty cleaning. The light-duty cleaners that are nontoxic and nonflammable must be used whenever possible.

notes.front: Inside the aircraft, how can a dropped bolt or bit of wire cause corrosion?
notes.back: With moisture and dissimilar metal contact, it can cause electrolytic corrosion.
notes.explanation: Metal particles and other debris from structural work are to be cleaned up as soon as possible.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Interior Cleaning”, p. 8-24
notes.evidence: Nuts, bolts, bits of wire, or other metal objects carelessly dropped and neglected, combined with moisture and dissimilar metal contact, can cause electrolytic corrosion. When performing structural work inside the aircraft, clean up all metal particles and other debris as soon as possible.

notes.front: What flash point range do most high flash point solvents, such as Stoddard solvent, have?
notes.back: From 100 °F to 140 °F.
notes.explanation: They clean almost like gasoline but carry a fire hazard like unheated kerosene.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Flammable & Combustible Agents”, p. 8-25
notes.evidence: Specially refined petroleum products, first developed as “Stoddard solvent” and now sold under a variety of trade names by different companies, have solvent properties approximating gasoline, but have fire hazard properties similar to those of kerosene as commonly used (not heated). Most of these are stable products having a flash point from 100 °F to 140 °F

notes.front: Class I flammable liquids, with a flash point below 100 °F, are not to be used for aircraft cleaning. What are two that the handbook lists?
notes.back: Any two of: acetone, aviation gasoline, MEK, naphtha, toluol.
notes.explanation: Where a flammable liquid is absolutely necessary, one with a flash point of 100 °F or more is used instead.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Flammable & Combustible Agents”, p. 8-25
notes.evidence: Low flash point solvents—Class I (flash point at below 100 °F) flammable liquids are not to be used for aircraft cleaning or refurbishing. Common materials falling into this “class” are acetone, aviation gasoline (AVGAS), methyl ethyl ketone, naphtha, and toluol.

notes.front: During cabin cleaning with flammable liquids, what vapour level calls for emergency revision of operations?
notes.back: Above 25 percent of the lower flammability limit, measured 5 feet from where it is used.
notes.explanation: The measurement is taken 5 feet from where the liquid is being used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Fire Prevention Precautions”, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: The accumulation of flammable vapors above 25 percent of the lower flammability limit of the particular vapor being used, measured at a point 5 feet from the location of use, shall result in emergency revisions of operations in progress.

notes.front: What minimum flashpoint must aircraft cleaning solvents have to avoid explosion-proofing equipment and other special precautions?
notes.back: Not less than 105 °F.
notes.explanation: Chlorinated solvents meet the nonflammable requirement but are toxic.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Solvent Cleaners”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: In general, solvent cleaners used in aircraft cleaning must have a flashpoint of not less than 105 °F, if explosion proofing of equipment and other special precautions are to be avoided. Chlorinated solvents of all types meet the nonflammable requirements, but are toxic.

notes.front: A mechanic must degrease a part inside a small, closed baggage bay. Which solvent should not be used there?
notes.back: C: methyl ethyl ketone.
notes.choices:
A) A water-based cleaner
B) A detergent solution
C) Methyl ethyl ketone
D) Plain water
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are not low-flashpoint solvents.
notes.explanation: Its flashpoint is below 100 °F, which rules it out in a confined space; acetone is the circular’s other example.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-90a(14), p. 6-22
notes.evidence: (14) In confined location, do not use solvents with a low flashpoint (below 100 °F), such as methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) and acetone.

notes.front: Why must an air-cooled engine be kept free of grease and dirt?
notes.back: They insulate it against the cooling airflow.
notes.explanation: The build-up can also hide cracks and other defects.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Powerplant Cleaning”, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: Grease and dirt accumulations on an air-cooled engine provide an effective insulation against the cooling effect of air flowing over it. Such an accumulation can also cover up cracks or other defects.

notes.front: What is the drawback of dry cleaning (Stoddard) solvent before painting?
notes.back: It leaves a slight residue that may interfere with some final paint films.
notes.explanation: It is still preferable to kerosene for all cleaning.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Dry Cleaning Solvent”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: Dry cleaning solvent is preferable to kerosene for all cleaning purposes, but like kerosene, it leaves a slight residue upon evaporation that may interfere with the application of some final paint films.

notes.front: How do aliphatic and aromatic naphtha differ in use?
notes.back: Aliphatic wipes surfaces before painting and is safe on acrylics and rubber; aromatic is toxic and attacks them.
notes.explanation: Aliphatic naphtha still flashes at about 80 °F, so it needs care too.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Aliphatic and Aromatic Naphtha”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: Aliphatic naphtha is recommended for wipe down of cleaned surfaces just before painting. This material can also be used for cleaning acrylics and rubber. It flashes at approximately 80 °F and must be used with care. Aromatic naphtha must not be confused with the aliphatic material. It is toxic, attacks acrylics and rubber products

notes.front: What is safety solvent, and what did it replace?
notes.back: Trichloroethane (methyl chloroform), nonflammable in ordinary use; it replaced carbon tetrachloride.
notes.explanation: As a chlorinated solvent it needs the usual precautions; prolonged use can cause dermatitis.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Safety Solvent”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: Safety solvent, trichloroethane (methyl chloroform), is used for general cleaning and grease removal. It is nonflammable under ordinary circumstances and is used as a replacement for carbon tetrachloride. The use and safety precautions necessary when using chlorinated solvents must be observed. Prolonged use can cause dermatitis on some persons.

notes.front: A mechanic cleans a steel part with kerosene and plans to leave it. What should follow?
notes.back: D: a coating or rinse with another protective agent.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, kerosene protects metal
B) A second kerosene wash
C) Painting straight over the film
D) A coating or rinse with another protective agent, as kerosene can leave a corrosive film
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: kerosene leaves a film that may be corrosive. C paints over that film.
notes.explanation: It evaporates slowly and leaves an appreciable film that may actually be corrosive.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Kerosene”, p. 8-27
notes.evidence: It is also used for general solvent cleaning, but its use must be followed by a coating or rinse with some other type of protective agent. Kerosene does not evaporate as rapidly as dry cleaning solvent and generally leaves an appreciable film on cleaned surfaces that may actually be corrosive.

notes.front: Which abrasive is generally the first choice for removing corrosion products and light abrasive work?
notes.back: Nonwoven abrasive pads.
notes.explanation: They are clean and inexpensive and suit most metals, though one pad should not be used on different metals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Mild Abrasive Materials”, p. 8-28
notes.evidence: The introduction of various grades of nonwoven abrasive pads has given the AMT a clean, inexpensive material for the removal of corrosion products and for other light abrasive needs. The pads can be used on most metals (although the same pad should not be used on different metals) and are generally the first choice when the situation arises.

notes.front: Aluminium oxide paper of {{c1::300}} grit or finer is safe to use on most aircraft surfaces.
notes.explanation: Papers must not hold sharp, needlelike grains that embed themselves, nor abrasives that corrode the material.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Abrasive Papers”, p. 8-28
notes.evidence: Abrasive papers used on aircraft surfaces must not contain sharp or needlelike abrasives that can imbed themselves in the base metal being cleaned or in the protective coating being maintained. The abrasives used must not corrode the material being cleaned. Aluminum oxide paper, 300 grit or finer, is available in several forms and is safe to use on most surfaces.

notes.front: Why avoid carborundum (silicon carbide) paper, especially on aluminium or magnesium?
notes.back: Its sharp, very hard grains penetrate and bury themselves in the surface.
notes.explanation: The grains bury themselves even in steel, let alone the softer metals.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Abrasive Papers”, p. 8-29
notes.evidence: Avoid the use of carborundum (silicon carbide) papers, particularly on aluminum or magnesium. The grain structure of carborundum is sharp and the material is so hard that individual grains penetrate and bury themselves, even in steel surfaces.

notes.front: A mechanic reaches for emery paper to clean a magnesium gearbox cover. What is the risk?
notes.back: D: serious corrosion from imbedded iron oxide.
notes.choices:
A) None, emery is mild
B) Only scratching
C) Loss of the anodised film
D) Serious corrosion from imbedded iron oxide
notes.choicesExplained: A and B understate it. C: the cover is magnesium, and the handbook names iron oxide as the problem.
notes.explanation: Crocus cloth carries the same risk on aluminium or magnesium.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Abrasive Papers”, p. 8-29
notes.evidence: The use of emery paper or crocus cloth on aluminum or magnesium can cause serious corrosion of the metal by imbedded iron oxide.

notes.front: What can an alkaline cleaner do if it cannot be rinsed and neutralised effectively?
notes.back: Cause corrosion inside the lap joints of riveted or spot-welded sheet metal.
notes.explanation: Only cleaners that can be rinsed and neutralised effectively are to be used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Aircraft Cleaning”, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: As mentioned previously, cleaners that can be effectively rinsed and neutralized must be used, or an alkaline cleaner may cause corrosion within the lap joints of riveted or spot-welded sheet metal components.

notes.front: Why must all residues of chemical surface treatments be removed before painting?
notes.back: Their soluble salts liquefy and promote blistering in the paint.
notes.explanation: Chemical cleaners on assembled aircraft must be relatively neutral and easy to remove.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Chemical Cleaners”, p. 8-29
notes.evidence: Any materials used must be relatively neutral and easy to remove. It is emphasized that all residues must be removed. Soluble salts from chemical surface treatments, such as chromic acid or dichromate treatment, liquefy and promote blistering in the paint coatings.

notes.front: A mechanic wants to use a strong household cleaner on a polished aluminium skin with lap joints. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: A: choose a neutral pH product.
notes.choices:
A) Choose a neutral pH product, since many consumer products can cause corrosion if trapped in lap joints
B) Any cleaner is fine if rinsed
C) Use it undiluted to save time
D) Use steel wool with it
notes.choicesExplained: B: some consumer products are caustic enough to corrode when trapped. C makes it worse. D embeds steel in the aluminium.
notes.explanation: Trapped caustic cleaner between lap joints can itself start corrosion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Treatment of Unpainted Aluminum Surfaces”, p. 8-18
notes.evidence: Use caution when choosing a cleaner. Many commercial consumer products are actually caustic enough to induce corrosion if trapped between aluminum lap joints. Choose a neutral pH product.

notes.front: When rinsing loosened paint and stripper with a water spray, what pressure is used?
notes.back: A low to medium pressure stream.
notes.explanation: The water is aimed directly at the area being scrubbed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cleaning and Paint Removal”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: If water spray is available, use a low to medium pressure stream of water directly on the area being scrubbed.

notes.front: After an aircraft is recovered from water, what is the most important factor, and why is fresh water still a concern?
notes.back: Prompt action; fresh water may hold salt that concentrates and speeds attack as it dries.
notes.explanation: Sea water is more corrosive, but drying fresh water concentrates its salt too.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-220, p. 6-48
notes.evidence: a. Seawater, because of salt content, is more corrosive than freshwater. However, freshwater may also contain varying amounts of salt, and, as drying occurs, the salt concentration is increased and corrosive attack accelerated. b. Prompt action is the most important factor following recovery of an aircraft from water immersion.

notes.front: How does the circular’s primer method for installing a removable steel fastener work?
notes.back: Coat the fastener with primer and set and torque it while the primer is still wet.
notes.explanation: The primer is applied to the fastener itself, not just the hole.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-135b, p. 6-31
notes.evidence: (3) Apply a coating of primer to the fastener, and, while wet with primer, set and torque the fastener.

notes.front: A steel fitting will be riveted to aluminium structure. Which primer does the handbook prefer for the joint?
notes.back: B: epoxy primer.
notes.choices:
A) No primer
B) Epoxy primer
C) Zinc chromate only
D) Any enamel topcoat
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the dissimilar joint unprotected. C is allowed but not preferred. D is a finish, not the joint protection.
notes.explanation: Zinc chromate is acceptable, but epoxy is named as preferable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Contacts Not Involving Magnesium”, p. 8-20
notes.evidence: All dissimilar joints not involving magnesium are protected by the application of a minimum of two coats of zinc chromate or, preferably, epoxy primer in addition to normal primer requirements.

notes.front: The baked enamel on a magnesium engine case is damaged after corrosion treatment. What can restore protection in the field?
notes.back: C: a good air-drying enamel.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; the case must be scrapped
B) Wax only
C) A good air-drying enamel
D) Bare metal is acceptable
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are not what the circular says. B is not a protective topcoat here.
notes.explanation: Engine cases usually carry baked enamel rather than other top coat finishes.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, Section 9 (magnesium and magnesium alloys), p. 6-36
notes.evidence: Where engine cases are concerned, baked enamel overcoats are usually involved rather than other top coat finishes. A good air-drying enamel can be used to restore protection.

notes.front: In integral fuel cells, what should the top coat finish be inspected for?
notes.back: Breaks, peeling, lifting of the surface or other damage.
notes.explanation: Structure behind the finish is checked for pitting or intergranular corrosion damage too.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-76, p. 6-20
notes.evidence: a. Inspect top coat finish for breaks, peeling, lifting of surface, or other damage. b. Inspect aircraft structure for top coat finish damage from pitting or intergranular corrosion.

notes.front: What causes blushing in a doped finish, and above what humidity can it occur?
notes.back: Moisture condensing on the surface as thinner evaporates; above 65 percent humidity.
notes.explanation: Fast-evaporating thinner cools the surface enough for moisture to condense on it.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23a, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: The appearance of light shaded dull areas on the surface as dope dries is the result of moisture in the atmosphere condensing on a surface due to the cooling effect of the fast-evaporating components of dope thinner escaping from the coating. Blushing can occur at any temperature when the humidity is above 65 percent.

notes.front: A mechanic sprays finish on a hot afternoon, in direct sunlight with a breeze. The finish dries rough, like the skin of an orange. What caused it?
notes.back: D: fast solvent evaporation from sun, heat and draught.
notes.choices:
A) Too little air pressure only
B) Too many coats of primer
C) Humidity below 65 percent
D) Fast solvent evaporation from sun, heat and draught
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and B are not the conditions described. Low humidity is not a cause the circular lists.
notes.explanation: High air temperature and spraying in sun or wind both drive fast solvent evaporation.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23c, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: similar to the texture of an orange peel, may be caused by one or more of the following conditions: (1) Viscosity of material being sprayed is too high. (2) Air temperature is too high. (3) Spraying in direct sunlight, onto a hot surface or in a drafty/windy condition, which causes a fast solvent evaporation.

notes.front: In a doped fabric finish, what are pinholes, and what usually causes them?
notes.back: Voids between threads not filled by the first dope coats; usually improper dope application.
notes.explanation: Contamination such as oil or fingerprints can also cause them.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23b, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: Voids between the fabric threads that are not filled with the first coats of dope are called pinholes. They may be caused by fabric contamination, such as oil or fingerprints, but are usually the result of improper dope application.

notes.front: What is one cause of blisters in a sprayed finish?
notes.back: Any one of: hot sun to speed drying; too high air pressure; water or oil in the air supply.
notes.explanation: Each cause traps vapour, air or contamination in the film.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23d, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: (1) Freshly coated surface placed in hot sunlight or high temperature area to accelerate drying time, causing the vapor from rapidly evaporating solvents to be trapped. (2) Excessive high air pressure used to spray heavy coats which “blasts” air bubbles into the coating. (3) Water or oil in air supply.

notes.front: What are two causes of runs, sags and curtains in a sprayed finish?
notes.back: Any two of: viscosity too low; coats too heavy; too little drying time; gun too close; gun badly adjusted.
notes.explanation: The circular lists five causes, so any two are right.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23e, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: e. Runs, Sags, and Curtains. These defects may be caused by one or more of the following conditions: (1) Viscosity of material being sprayed is too low. (2) Coats applied too heavily. (3) Insufficient drying time between coats. (4) Spray gun held too close to work surface. (5) Improperly adjusted spray gun.

notes.front: On a humid day, light-shaded dull areas appear on dope as it dries. Which defect is this?
notes.back: B: blushing.
notes.choices:
A) Pinholes
B) Blushing
C) Orange peel
D) Runs and sags
notes.choicesExplained: A are voids between threads. C is a rough texture. D are flows from heavy or thin coats.
notes.explanation: The dull areas are condensed atmospheric moisture on the drying surface.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23a, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: Blushing. The appearance of light shaded dull areas on the surface as dope dries is the result of moisture in the atmosphere condensing on a surface

notes.front: When mixing acid and water, which goes into which?
notes.back: Always add acid to water, never water to acid.
notes.explanation: Chemicals are otherwise mixed per the manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 6-90a(2), p. 6-21
notes.evidence: (1) Avoid prolonged breathing of solvent or acid vapors. (2) Never add water to acid. Always add acid to water. (3) Mix all chemicals per the manufacturer’s instructions.

notes.front: What protective equipment is worn when using paint stripper?
notes.back: Rubber gloves, acid-repellent aprons and goggles.
notes.explanation: Stripper is toxic and harms both skin and eyes.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cleaning and Paint Removal”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: Paint stripper is toxic and contains ingredients harmful to both skin and eyes. Therefore, wear rubber gloves, aprons of acid repellent material, and goggle type eyeglasses.

notes.front: A container label for a surface treatment warns only that it is toxic. The mechanic plans to store it beside paint thinner. What should they check first?
notes.back: D: the Safety Data Sheet.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more, the label is enough
B) Only the expiry date
C) The colour of the liquid
D) The Safety Data Sheet, as some treatments react violently with thinners
notes.choicesExplained: A: labels may not list every hazard of mixing. B and C say nothing about incompatibility.
notes.explanation: A label may be too small to list every hazard of mixing with incompatible substances.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Chemical Surface Treatment and Inhibitors”, p. 8-22
notes.evidence: The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) should also be consulted for information. For example, some chemicals used in surface treatments react violently if inadvertently mixed with paint thinners.

notes.front: When refinishing a balanced control surface, how much paint may be applied?
notes.back: No more coats than the manufacturer originally applied.
notes.explanation: The circular gives special emphasis to the effect of too many extra coats on balanced control surfaces.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 4-36b
notes.evidence: b. Painting and Refinishing. Special emphasis is directed to the effect of too many extra coats of paint on balanced control surfaces. Mechanics must avoid adding additional coats of paint in excess of what the manufacturer originally applied.

notes.front: An aileron has been stripped and repainted with two more coats than the factory used. What is the risk, and what should be done?
notes.back: D: upset balance, which could be a serious flight hazard.
notes.choices:
A) None, paint weighs nothing
B) Galvanic corrosion at the hinge
C) Only a colour mismatch
D) Upset control surface balance, which could be a serious flight hazard
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the weight of paint. C is cosmetic. B is not an effect of extra paint.
notes.explanation: Balance outside the allowable value could be a serious flight hazard.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 4-36a–b
notes.evidence: Failure to check and retain control surface balance within the original or maximum allowable value could result in a serious flight hazard. b. Painting and Refinishing. Special emphasis is directed to the effect of too many extra coats of paint on balanced control surfaces.

notes.front: How should a spray gun be adjusted for a smooth finish?
notes.back: To a uniform pattern, atomising the material into fine, wet particles.
notes.explanation: Fine, wet particles merge into a smooth film.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B with Change 1, para. 2-23c, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: The spray gun should be adjusted to a uniform spray pattern with the material atomized to deposit fine, wet particles that merge and form a smooth film.

notes.front: How must stripped paint residue be disposed of?
notes.back: In accordance with environmental laws.
notes.explanation: Rinsing must be complete, and what it carries away is still regulated waste.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Surface Cleaning and Paint Removal”, p. 8-15
notes.evidence: On small areas, any method may be used that assures complete rinsing of the cleaned area. Use care to dispose of the stripped residue in accordance with environmental laws.

notes.front: How must nationality and registration marks normally be applied to an aircraft?
notes.back: Painted on, or affixed by other means giving similar permanence.
notes.explanation: Removable marks are allowed only in the cases paragraph (d) lists.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 45 (1 January 2025 edition), § 45.21(c)(1)
notes.evidence: (c) Aircraft nationality and registration marks must— (1) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, be painted on the aircraft or affixed by any other means insuring a similar degree of permanence;

notes.front: May nationality and registration marks carry ornamentation?
notes.back: No: they must have no ornamentation.
notes.explanation: The marks must also contrast in colour with the background and be legible.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 45 (1 January 2025 edition), § 45.21(c)(2)
notes.evidence: (2) Have no ornamentation; (3) Contrast in color with the background; and (4) Be legible.

notes.front: Apart from permanence, no ornamentation and colour contrast, what is the fourth requirement § 45.21(c) sets for registration marks?
notes.back: They must be legible.
notes.explanation: All four apply to every mark, whatever its size.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 45 (1 January 2025 edition), § 45.21(c)(4)
notes.evidence: (c) Aircraft nationality and registration marks must— (1) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, be painted on the aircraft or affixed by any other means insuring a similar degree of permanence; (2) Have no ornamentation; (3) Contrast in color with the background; and (4) Be legible.

notes.front: What must the marks on a United States-registered aircraft consist of?
notes.back: The Roman capital letter N followed by the aircraft’s registration number.
notes.explanation: Any suffix letters must also be Roman capitals.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 45 (1 January 2025 edition), § 45.23(a)
notes.evidence: (a) Each operator of an aircraft must display on that aircraft marks consisting of the Roman capital letter ‘‘N’’ (denoting United States registration) followed by the registration number of the aircraft. Each suffix letter used in the marks displayed must also be a Roman capital letter.

notes.front: After repainting, an owner wants a stripe to run through the registration number, making it hard to read. What does part 45 say?
notes.back: B: not without authorisation.
notes.choices:
A) It is fine if the stripe is thin
B) No design that modifies or confuses the marks may be placed without authorisation from the Federal Aviation Administration
C) It is fine on the tail only
D) It is fine on experimental aircraft
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D invent exceptions the rule does not contain.
notes.explanation: The rule forbids any design, mark or symbol that modifies or confuses the marks unless authorised.
notes.source: 14 CFR part 45 (1 January 2025 edition), § 45.21(b)
notes.evidence: (b) Unless otherwise authorized by the FAA, no person may place on any aircraft a design, mark, or symbol that modifies or confuses the nationality and registration marks.
